ulrich.name: Ulrich
ulrich.role: owns the incubator house, takes ten percent

mack.name: Mack
mack.role: the CEO the board brought in

episodes.title: Viral
episodes.borrowed: The live stream that goes huge while Anton overheats in the garage and the team scrambles to keep it alive

cold_open.say: Everybody up. Everybody. A chef with nine million followers just posted about us.
She says Forkcast found her a table in thirty seconds. We've had four thousand sign-ups since dinner.
Why is the garage making that noise?
Because Forkcast lives in the garage now. I moved it to Aleister last night.
We were paying a stranger to do my job badly. Aleister is fine. He's just warm.
He's warm like a toaster is warm. That's a desk fan, Gilroy.
Yes, hello, Ulrich Bachner. The incubator. Did I see it coming? I designed it coming.

brief.say: She's posting again tomorrow at eight, in the Friday dinner rush, to people who'll be awake this time.
The garage won't make it to eight. I say that with love.
Good news! I've written a plan. It's called Make Forkcast Web-Scale. I'm very proud of it.

cards.label: Move to the cloud
cards.plain: Rent an app server and a managed Postgres database, and move Forkcast out of the garage.

takes.say: You'd be paying someone to babysit a server I already babysit.
Gilroy, the server is on fire. A little bit. In places.

cards.label: Kubernetes
cards.plain: Split Forkcast into twelve small services running on a container cluster.

takes.say: It's how Hubbub does it. If we're going to do it, we should do it right.
Twelve things to break instead of one, for a team of five. Bold.

cards.label: Add a cache
cards.plain: Keep copies of recent answers in Redis so the database isn't asked the same thing over and over. I've set everything to one hour!

takes.say: Caches make everything faster. That's just science.
A cache is a machine for telling people things that used to be true.

cards.label: CDN for photos
cards.plain: Serve photos and scripts from servers near each diner instead of from our app.

takes.say: Every page has fourteen photos of risotto. Get them off our server.
And when a restaurant changes its photos? Oh, they can be an hour old. Lovely.

cards.label: Queue sign-up work
cards.plain: Put welcome emails and other sign-up chores in a queue, and let a worker get through them.

takes.say: Each sign-up waits while we send its welcome email. Fifteen thousand at once is a lot of waiting.
Nobody needs their welcome email this exact second.

cards.label: Rewrite in Rust
cards.plain: Rewrite the booking code in Rust. Rust is very fast!

takes.say: Serious companies rewrite in Rust. It's practically a funding round.
The app isn't slow. It's waiting for the database. You'd be speeding up the waiting.

cards.label: Forty servers
cards.plain: Forty app servers. Small ones, but forty.

takes.say: Hubbub has forty thousand servers. Forty is the least we can do. More servers, more fast.
Ulrich, every one of those talks to the same database, and the database can only...

cards.label: Add an index
cards.plain: Add an index on bookings by restaurant and night, so finding tonight's tables doesn't read every booking.

takes.say: Like the index in a book. Thirty minutes of work.
Boring. Correct. My favourite combination.

cards.label: Cache AI answers
cards.plain: Answer popular questions from a cache, and use prompt caching so the long fixed start of each prompt is billed at a fraction.

takes.say: Half our searches are 'date night in the Mission'. We shouldn't pay for that answer twice.
The answers can be an hour old. Restaurants don't move.

cards.label: Shard by city
cards.plain: Split the database into one per city. Very web-scale!

takes.say: We're in one city, but we could be in more cities! Later!
I've seen a sharding project before. I was much younger when it started.

cards.label: Biggest AI model
cards.plain: Switch the concierge to the biggest model there is.

takes.say: Five times the price per answer, but five times the... vibes?
The answers were fine. The bill was the problem.

reply.say: I measured last night. The database was at a hundred percent, almost all of it on 'free tables near me tonight'.
It reads every booking we've ever had. Every time. We need an index.
Menus and photos change about once a day. An hour old is fine.
Tonight's free tables change every couple of minutes. An hour old is a lie.
And 'My bookings' is different for every person.

asks.text: Is this cache per user or shared?

reply.say: Shared! Everyone gets the same copy. Of everything. Including 'My bookings'.
Oh.
That happened at a company I used to work for. Everyone saw everyone's bookings. I still dream about it.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: The model calls are four fifths of the bill. And the provider caps how many we can make a minute.
I can cache AI answers! I should have thought of that.
Web-scale! My favourite. I'll shard the database by city!
The smartest one! Diners will feel the difference. Your accountant will too.

hotfixes.label: Add another app server
hotfixes.say: Traffic just doubled! Hotfix: add another app server? It's {monthly} a month.

corner.say: Aleister is down. Get the other fan. GET THE OTHER FAN.
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The database is reading every booking again. And again.
People keep picking tables that went a minute ago.
A diner in Oakland can see someone's anniversary booking. This is the dream again.
Why does everyone keep getting logged out?
Forty servers, one database, a hundred connections. Do the maths, Ulrich.
The model provider is turning our searches away.
Fifteen thousand sign-ups, all waiting on welcome emails.
We're serving every risotto photo ourselves.
Twelve thousand users. TWELVE. I'm texting everyone I know.

garage_melt.title: Aleister overheated and shut down.
garage_melt.plain: One server in a garage ran the app and the database together. Past its limit it got hot, switched itself off, and Forkcast went with it.

full_scan.title: The database read every booking ever made, every time.
full_scan.plain: Finding tonight's free tables meant reading the whole bookings table, and every new booking made the next search longer.
full_scan.term: a full table scan; the fix is an index
full_scan.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add an index for this query.

no_cache.title: The database answered the same menu questions thousands of times.
no_cache.plain: Menus barely change, but every page asked the database for them again.
no_cache.tell_ai: Cache this. How stale can it be?

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Add a server, and make the servers stateless.

no_cdn.title: Our own servers were sending every photo.
no_cdn.plain: Photos and scripts are most of what a page weighs, and our app was serving all of them.
no_cdn.tell_ai: Serve static files from a CDN.

no_queue.title: Fifteen thousand sign-ups hit the app at once.
no_queue.plain: Every sign-up held a server while it sent the welcome email, a slow call to an email service. That could have waited in a line.
no_queue.tell_ai: Put work that can wait on a queue.

stale_tables.title: Diners booked tables that were already taken.
stale_tables.plain: The cache kept tonight's tables too long. They change every couple of minutes, so diners kept picking tables that had gone.

cache_leak.title: Diners saw other people's bookings.
cache_leak.plain: 'My bookings' went into a shared cache, so one diner's page was handed to everyone who came next. That's a data breach.
cache_leak.term: per-user data in a shared cache
cache_leak.tell_ai: Is this cache per user or shared?

stateless.title: Diners kept getting logged out.
stateless.plain: Each server remembered logins in its own memory. With more than one server, the next request often landed on one that had never met you.
stateless.tell_ai: Make the servers stateless: keep sessions in Redis.

too_many_connections.title: Most servers couldn't reach the database.
too_many_connections.plain: Every server holds ten connections to the database, and our Postgres allows a hundred. Forty servers wanted four hundred.
too_many_connections.term: the connection limit; a connection pooler shares them
too_many_connections.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

ai_bill.title: The AI bill hit five figures in one night.
ai_bill.plain: Every search paid for a fresh answer, even the thousandth 'date night in the Mission'.
ai_bill.tell_ai: Cache AI answers, and use prompt caching.

big_model.title: The biggest model cost five times as much.
big_model.plain: The answers didn't need it. The bill noticed.
big_model.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.plain: A nearby copy of an answer, so you don't work it out again. Ask how stale it can be, and whose it is: per-user data is cached per user, never shared.
Find the bottleneck first. Then a bigger server, or more servers behind a load balancer, kept stateless so any of them can take any request. Most apps never need much more.

lines.say: Fifty thousand users! I want to see them. All of them. On a screen. Updating every hour.
In the boardroom. By Monday. Make it huge.

episodes.title: The Board Meeting
episodes.borrowed: Richard pushed out as CEO by the board, and Jack Barker's box

cold_open.say: Fifty thousand users! Where's my screen? I said a screen. I said huge.
We've voted. Forkcast needs an experienced CEO.
This is Mack Barlow. He's run three companies.
Four. One was a boat. Love the energy in this room. Love the little app.
As a board member, I voted for Mack. As your mentor, I voted with a heavy heart. Both were yes.
You stay on as Head of Product. You keep the robot. I'll handle the vision.
Two things. A dashboard on every screen in this building, live. And a box.

brief.say: The board comes back Friday night to watch the dinner rush on the big screen. With prospects. Box prospects.
A normal busy Friday: fifteen thousand diners at the peak. Bookings have to keep working while the board watches.
I've written a plan! It's called Dashboards For Everyone. Every number, live, every minute!

cards.label: Board dashboard
cards.plain: Forty live tiles on the boardroom screen and the board's laptops, straight from our database, refreshing every minute!

takes.say: Forty tiles! Can it be forty-one? Is forty-one bigger?
Every tile is a question for the database. Every screen, every minute. I'm only asking.

cards.label: Biggest database
cards.plain: Move Postgres to the biggest size there is: eight times the power, for eight times the price.

takes.say: Bigger is faster. I don't see the debate.
It'd work. It's also thirty-two hundred dollars a month, every month, for a screen.

cards.label: Read replica
cards.plain: A live copy of the database just for the dashboard, so its questions don't slow down bookings.

takes.say: A replica keeps the dashboard off the bookings. That part's real.
It's a copy of the same kind of database. Same huge questions, same slow answers, now in a second place.

cards.label: The Box
cards.plain: Sell every restaurant a Forkcast server for its back office. Hardware! Margins! A box!

takes.say: Investors understand boxes. You can hold a box. You can't hold a cloud.
We'd be fixing two hundred servers in two hundred restaurant basements. With our hands.

cards.label: Analytics DB
cards.plain: Copy the bookings every hour into a separate database built for big questions, and point the dashboard at that.

takes.say: You don't do the accounts at the front desk. At my last company the numbers had their own room. I had it painted.
I've checked it twice. He's right. Somebody write down the date.

cards.label: Error alerts
cards.plain: Track errors in the app and in every scheduled job, and message us the moment one fails.

takes.say: At a previous company we found out things were broken from the news.
Alerts are for people who write bugs.

cards.label: Real-time stream
cards.plain: Stream every booking into the analytics database the moment it happens, on a managed event-streaming cluster.

takes.say: Real time is the only time.
Chaz asked for hourly. That's three thousand a month for the other fifty-nine minutes.

cards.label: Two hundred tiles
cards.plain: Every number we have, on one enormous wall. Two hundred tiles!

takes.say: Now THAT is a dashboard.
Which of these numbers would change what we do?

asks.text: Is this OLTP or OLAP work?

reply.say: The app does lots of tiny jobs. Book this table, show my bookings. That's OLTP: the front desk.
Every tile asks a huge question across everything we've ever stored. That's OLAP: the accountant's office.
Two hundred and forty of those a minute, on the database that takes the bookings.

asks.text: How fresh do the numbers need to be?

reply.say: The board meets four times a year.
Chaz asked for every hour. An hour old is plenty for a board.

asks.text: How will we know if it breaks?

reply.say: Know? We'll... someone will mention it?
At a previous company we learned the payroll job had stopped when the pay stopped. I'd like alerts, please.
Alerts! Great idea. Mine now.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: The biggest database costs eight times as much, whatever the traffic. That's forever, not just Friday.
The dashboard asks the same questions at any traffic. More diners just means more rows to add up.
Real-time! I'll stream every booking as it happens. It's only a small cluster. Of servers. That we run.
Huge! Chaz's favourite word. Two hundred tiles, coming up!

events.banner: The board is watching the big screen

hotfixes.label: Fix and rerun the copy
hotfixes.say: Alert! The 8pm copy into the analytics database just failed: a restaurant put a noodle emoji in its name. Hotfix: handle it and rerun?

corner.say: Every time the board's screen refreshes, somebody's booking waits behind it.
Bookings are fine. The replica's drowning. The board's screen just says 'Loading'.
Two hundred tiles. The analytics database is turning them away.
Why does the big screen still say seven o'clock? Did we break time?
The screen says we've had nine bookings tonight. Nine. The prospects are looking at me.
The database is maxed out.
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The model provider is turning our searches away.
Look at it go! Fifteen thousand! I'm screenshotting everything!

no_dashboard.title: There was no dashboard.
no_dashboard.plain: The board asked for one screen of numbers and got none. The bookings were fine; the board meeting wasn't.
no_dashboard.tell_ai: Build what the board asked for, as simply as it works.

olap_on_oltp.title: The board's dashboard slowed down the bookings.
olap_on_oltp.plain: Every tile asked a huge question across everything we've ever stored, again every minute, on the same database taking Friday's bookings. Bookings waited behind the board's questions.
olap_on_oltp.term: OLAP work on an OLTP database
olap_on_oltp.tell_ai: Is this OLTP or OLAP work? Put the analytics in a data warehouse.

replica_slow.title: The replica couldn't answer the dashboard.
replica_slow.plain: The copy kept the bookings safe, but it's the same kind of database, built for lots of small, quick questions. The dashboard's huge ones swamped it, and the board's screen timed out.
replica_slow.term: a read replica is still an OLTP database
replica_slow.tell_ai: Is this OLTP or OLAP work?

too_many_tiles.title: Two hundred tiles swamped the analytics database.
too_many_tiles.plain: Every tile is a question, and every screen asks it again every minute. Two hundred was more than our small analytics database could answer, and nobody could read them all anyway.
too_many_tiles.tell_ai: Show the few numbers that change a decision.

silent_failure.title: The 8pm copy job broke, and stayed broken.
silent_failure.plain: A restaurant's name broke the hourly copy into the analytics database. Nobody fixed it and ran it again, so the board's numbers stopped at 7pm and stayed there.
silent_failure.term: a failed pipeline job; alerts tell you, then someone fixes it
silent_failure.tell_ai: How will we know if it breaks? Add error tracking and alerts.

stale_numbers.title: The board watched last night's numbers.
stale_numbers.plain: The copy into the analytics database ran once a night, at 3am, so all Friday evening the big screen showed the morning's numbers.
stale_numbers.tell_ai: How fresh do the numbers need to be?

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Add a server, and make the servers stateless.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

lessons.plain: The app's database is the front desk: lots of small, quick jobs. Big questions across everything go to a separate copy built for them, a data warehouse, kept up to date by copying new data across in regular batches.
Once it's live, you can't watch every screen and every job. Error tracking and alerts tell you something broke, ideally before your customers, or your board, do.

lines.say: Great news. Hubbub called. They loved the dashboard.
They asked a lot of questions about how Forkcast works. I answered all of them. In detail. With slides.
